item.title: [GitHub Pages 獨立網域 #1] 告別免費 github.io：使用 Porkbun + Cloudflare 綁定自訂網域 (CNAME 扁平化與免費 SSL)
item.description: 徹底告別免費 github.io 二級子網域，透過 Porkbun 購買頂級網域並委派至 Cloudflare Anycast DNS，利用 CNAME 扁平化 (Flattening) 達成 GitHub Pages 零停機平滑遷移，解決 Docusaurus CNAME 自動重設難題的完整工程實戰。
item.content:encoded:
對於技術開發者而言，利用 GitHub Pages 的免費二級子網域（username.github.io/project）架設部落格幾乎是零成本的最佳入門選擇。只需一次 Git Push，即可透過全球 CDN 免費分發靜態頁面，完全無需維護底層伺服器。

然而，一旦你計劃打造具有專業影響力的技術品牌並開啟 Google AdSense（谷歌廣告聯盟）流量變現 時，就會遭遇一道無法逾越的規則紅線：Google AdSense 嚴格禁止針對 *.github.io 等免費二級子網域提交網站審查。此外，搜尋引擎累積的網域權重（Domain Authority）也無法沉澱為個人數位資產。要想通過商業化審查並沉澱 SEO 資產，擁有獨立的**頂級根網域（Apex Custom Domain，例如 globaldevlog.com）**是必經之路。

作為靜態網站工程化系列的第一篇，本文將以我們的技術部落格從 jbjihwan.github.io/global_blog 遷移至 https://globaldevlog.com 的實戰經歷為基礎，詳細拆解由 Porkbun + Cloudflare + GitHub Pages 構建的高可用三層生產架構與 DNS 深度配置要點。

1. 架構設計哲學：三層專業化高可用體系​

初學者在為 GitHub Pages 綁定獨立網域時，最常規的做法是在網域名稱註冊商處將 A 記錄 直接指向 GitHub 的 4 個固定 IP（185.199.108.153 等）。

這種傳統模式雖然簡單，但存在明顯的生產運維缺陷：

  • 缺乏邊緣層 DDoS 攻擊防護與惡意爬蟲清洗；
  • 遭遇故障或底層遷移時，DNS 生效速度緩慢；
  • 無法對靜態資源（CSS/JS/圖片）進行靈活的邊緣 CDN 快取調優。

為此，我們將職責解耦為三個專業化的服務層級：

層級選用服務核心職責與入選理由
1. 網域註冊商 (Registrar)Porkbun頂級網域首購與每年續費價格全網極具優勢，終身免費贈送 WHOIS 隱私保護，無套路加價
2. 邊緣 DNS 與安全層Cloudflare全球超低延遲 Anycast DNS，根網域 CNAME 扁平化 (Flattening)，免費 Universal SSL，自動化強制 HTTPS
3. 靜態託管源站GitHub Pages承載由 Docusaurus 編譯產生的純靜態產物，gh-pages 分支自動化部署，零伺服器成本

2. 第一步：Porkbun 網域購買與 Cloudflare 權威名稱伺服器委派​

  1. 網域選購：在 Porkbun 檢索並購買心儀的頂級根網域（如 globaldevlog.com）。
  2. 接入 Cloudflare：登入 Cloudflare 控制台，點擊 [新增網站] 輸入該網域，方案選擇 Free (免費版)。
  3. 獲取分配的名稱伺服器：Cloudflare 會自動分配一對專有的權威 Nameservers，例如： 
    roan.ns.cloudflare.com
    sneh.ns.cloudflare.com
  4. 修改 Porkbun DNS 委派：進入 Porkbun 的網域管理面板，找到 Authoritative Nameservers 設定項，刪除 Porkbun 預設地址，填入 Cloudflare 分配的 2 個伺服器地址並儲存。通常在 5 到 15 分鐘內全球生效。

3. 第二步：Cloudflare CNAME 扁平化 (Flattening) 與 Full SSL 模式​

按照 DNS 國際標準（RFC 1034），根網域（@）必須包含 SOA 和 NS 記錄，因此傳統上無法直接配置 CNAME 記錄。

Cloudflare 的 CNAME 扁平化 (CNAME Flattening) 技術徹底解決了這一痛點：在 DNS 解析查詢時，Cloudflare 邊緣節點會在底層即時解析目標地址（username.github.io）對應的 IP，並以 A 記錄 的形式直接向客戶端應答，從而讓根網域完美享有 CNAME 的所有敏捷特性。

A. 配置 Cloudflare DNS 解析記錄​

在 Cloudflare 儀表板 [DNS] > [記錄] 中，新增以下兩條開啟代理的記錄：

類型 (Type)名稱 (Name)目標 (Target)代理狀態 (Proxy status)TTL
CNAME@jbjihwan.github.io已代理 (點亮橘色雲朵)自動
CNAMEwwwjbjihwan.github.io已代理 (點亮橘色雲朵)自動

必須點亮橘色雲朵：只有處於代理模式下，造訪流量才會經由 Cloudflare 全球 Anycast 節點接入，享受自動化邊緣 SSL 終結、Brotli 極速壓縮以及抗 DDOS 保護。

B. 設定 SSL/TLS 加密模式​

前往 Cloudflare 左側導覽列 [SSL/TLS] > [概述]：

  • 將加密模式設為 Full (完全) 或 Full (Strict) (完全嚴格)；
  • 確保從訪客瀏覽器到 Cloudflare、以及從 Cloudflare 到 GitHub Pages 源站的端到端 HTTPS 雙向鏈路均得到高強度加密。

4. 第三步：更新 Docusaurus 核心配置 (docusaurus.config.ts)​

當部落格從子目錄路徑（/global_blog/）整體遷移至獨立根網域時，必須相應修正 docusaurus.config.ts：

const config: Config = {
  title: 'Global Dev Blog',
  tagline: 'Engineering Deep Dives in AI, Robotics, Computer Vision',

  // 替換為全新的頂級自訂網域
  url: 'https://globaldevlog.com',
  // 從子目錄 '/global_blog/' 改為頂級根路徑 '/'
  baseUrl: '/',

  organizationName: 'jbjihwan',
  projectName: 'global_blog',
  trailingSlash: false,
  // ...
};

5. 第四步：徹底攻克 GitHub Pages 部署後網域被重設的隱蔽陷阱 (static/CNAME)​

在配置 GitHub Pages 自訂網域時，幾乎所有開發者都踩過這個著名的“大坑”：

  1. 在 GitHub 儲存庫頁面的 Settings > Pages > Custom domain 中手動填入 globaldevlog.com 並儲存生效；
  2. 本地寫完新文章，終端執行 npm run deploy 重新部署；
  3. 部署一完成，重新整理 GitHub 頁面發現自訂網域輸入框再次變成了空白，線上網站瞬間爆出 404 錯誤或 SSL 憑證失效警告！

陷阱根源​

Docusaurus 的發布指令碼在編譯完成後，會將 build/ 目錄強制推送到 gh-pages 分支（git push --force）。如果該打包產物的根目錄下缺少純文字 CNAME 檔案，GitHub 會預設判定使用者已主動取消了自訂網域綁定。

永久解決方案​

在專案的 static/ 目錄下建立一個名為 CNAME 的純文字檔案（無任何副檔名），內容僅寫入一行你的網域：

globaldevlog.com

由於 Docusaurus 在建構時會自動將 static/ 目錄下的所有檔案原封不動複製到打包輸出根目錄，因此每次執行部署時，CNAME 檔案都會被永久提交至 gh-pages 分支的最頂層，網域綁定永不丟失。

6. 生產環境連通性驗證​

在專案根目錄下執行部署指令：

npm run deploy

部署成功後，在終端機透過 curl 命令驗證 HTTP 狀態碼與 SSL 憑證鏈回應：

curl -I https://globaldevlog.com
# HTTP/2 200
# server: cloudflare
# strict-transport-security: max-age=31536000

curl -I https://www.globaldevlog.com
# HTTP/2 200 (或 301 重新導向至根網域)

🔜 下篇預告​

獨立網域成功上線後，真正的商業化與多引擎搜尋獲客工作才剛剛拉開序幕：

  • 第二篇：[靜態網站商業化 #2] Docusaurus 接入 Google AdSense 審查實戰：解決 ads.txt 404 爬取故障與非同步指令碼安全植入
  • 第三篇：[全球多搜尋引擎 SEO #3] Google、Naver 與 Bing 站長平台權威配置：Sitemap 無法刪除之謎與主機層級報錯排查

item.title: From GitHub Pages to Custom Domain: Complete Guide to Porkbun, Cloudflare DNS, AdSense Approval, and Multi-Engine SEO
item.description: A comprehensive production blueprint for migrating a static Docusaurus blog on GitHub Pages to an apex custom domain via Porkbun and Cloudflare DNS, securing Google AdSense verification, and mastering multi-search engine SEO across Google, Naver, and Bing.
item.content:encoded:
Hosting a developer blog on GitHub Pages under username.github.io/project is one of the quickest ways to share technical insights. However, as your readership grows and you prepare for professional monetization, you hit a hard architectural wall: Google AdSense strictly prohibits free subdomains like *.github.io. To qualify for AdSense publisher verification, establish domain equity, and secure multi-region organic reach, you need your own apex custom domain.

Migrating a static documentation or engineering site to a custom domain is not just a DNS record change. It involves coordinating registrar name delegation, edge SSL termination, canonical redirects, automated publisher ads.txt hosting, and navigating subtle search console UI quirks across global and regional search engines.

In this guide, we break down our end-to-end migration from jbjihwan.github.io/global_blog to https://globaldevlog.com, including our zero-downtime DNS architecture, AdSense integration, and actionable solutions for real-world indexing traps in Google Search Console, Naver Search Advisor, and Bing Webmaster Tools.

1. Architectural Strategy: Porkbun + Cloudflare + GitHub Pages​

When connecting an apex domain (e.g., globaldevlog.com) to GitHub Pages, the traditional method uses raw A records pointing to GitHub's four Anycast IPs (185.199.108.153, etc.). While functional, this lacks modern edge security, DDoS filtering, and automatic HTTPS certificate renewal.

We adopted a high-availability 3-tier architecture:

TierProviderCore Responsibilities
RegistrarPorkbunDomain acquisition, WHOIS privacy protection, DNSSEC, authoritative NS delegation
Edge DNS & SecurityCloudflareGlobal Anycast DNS, CNAME Flattening on apex (@), Universal SSL Edge certificate, Bot Fight mode
Origin SSGGitHub PagesStatic artifact hosting compiled by Docusaurus, zero server maintenance, branch synchronization (gh-pages)

Porkbun NameServer Delegation​

In the Porkbun management console, replace default registrar nameservers with Cloudflare's assigned edge nameservers:

NS: roan.ns.cloudflare.com
NS: sneh.ns.cloudflare.com

Cloudflare CNAME Flattening Setup​

Apex domains (@) traditionally do not support CNAME records per RFC 1034. Cloudflare resolves this via CNAME Flattening, seamlessly resolving @ to GitHub Pages:

  • Type: CNAME | Name: @ | Target: jbjihwan.github.io | Proxy status: Proxied
  • Type: CNAME | Name: www | Target: jbjihwan.github.io | Proxy status: Proxied
  • SSL/TLS Mode: Set to Full (or Full Strict) to guarantee end-to-end HTTPS encryption.

2. Docusaurus Configuration Migration​

To transition cleanly from subpath routing (/global_blog/) to the domain root (/), update docusaurus.config.ts:

const config: Config = {
  title: 'Global Dev Blog',
  url: 'https://globaldevlog.com',
  baseUrl: '/',
  organizationName: 'jbjihwan',
  projectName: 'global_blog',
  trailingSlash: false,
  // ...
};

Static CNAME File​

GitHub Pages requires a plain text CNAME file located at the web root of your deployment branch. Place it in static/CNAME:

globaldevlog.com

During npm run deploy, Docusaurus automatically copies everything from static/ to the build root, informing GitHub's routing engine to map all incoming traffic for globaldevlog.com to this repository.

3. Google AdSense Approval Setup for Static Sites​

Google AdSense approval requires verifying site ownership, confirming an active publisher script, and crawling a root ads.txt file.

A. Publisher Script Injection​

In docusaurus.config.ts, inject the Google AdSense loader script asynchronously:

  scripts: [
    {
      src: 'https://pagead2.googlesyndication.com/pagead/js/adsbygoogle.js?client=ca-pub-4654073335496617',
      async: true,
      crossorigin: 'anonymous',
    },
  ],

B. Direct Root ads.txt Deployment​

Place your verified publisher credentials in static/ads.txt:

google.com, pub-4654073335496617, DIRECT, f08c47fec0942fa0

Verify live deployment immediately via curl or browser:

curl -I https://globaldevlog.com/ads.txt
# HTTP/2 200
# content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

4. Multi-Search Engine SEO & Real-World Troubleshooting​

Submitting sitemaps across multiple engines reveals distinct platform quirks and hidden UI traps. Here is how to conquer them:

A. Google Search Console: The Sitemap Delete Trap​

When submitting localized sitemaps (sitemap.xml, ko/sitemap.xml, ja/sitemap.xml, es/sitemap.xml), accidental typos (such as submitting the root URL https://globaldevlog.com/ as a sitemap) can create permanent "Has errors" notices.

Many developers click the three vertical dots (⋮) on the table row, only to find "See page indexing" disabled with no option to delete.

The Fix:

  1. Do not rely on the table row menu. Click directly on the sitemap URL text/row itself to open the Sitemap Details View.
  2. In the top-right corner of the details screen, click the header's three dots (⋮).
  3. Click [Remove sitemap] to purge the erroneous entry.
  4. For temporary "Couldn't fetch" errors (e.g., during DNS propagation), re-entering the path in "Add a new sitemap" triggers an immediate re-fetch and turns the status to Success.

B. Naver Search Advisor: "URL을 호스트 단위로 입력해주세요"​

Naver dominates Korean search traffic. When registering on Naver Search Advisor:

  1. Host-Level Error: Attempting to submit https://globaldevlog.com/sitemap.xml in the initial "사이트 등록" screen triggers a popup: "URL을 호스트 단위로 입력해주세요". This screen is only for domain registration (https://globaldevlog.com).
  2. Dual Ownership Verification: Deploy both the HTML verification file (static/naver<hash>.html) and the meta tag in themeConfig.metadata: 
    metadata: [
      { name: 'naver-site-verification', content: 'f04ea0b38166c1e280ce8e18acef37093b75f383' },
    ],
  3. Submitting Sitemaps & RSS: Inside Site Management (사이트 목록 > click your domain):
    • Navigate to [요청] > [사이트맵 제출]: enter sitemap.xml
    • Navigate to [요청] > [RSS 제출]: enter https://globaldevlog.com/blog/rss.xml
  4. Accelerating Yeti Bot: Under [요청] > [웹 페이지 수집], submit priority paths (blog, ko/blog, and latest posts) to trigger immediate crawling.

C. Bing Webmaster Tools & AI Copilot / ChatGPT Ingestion​

Bing Webmaster Tools powers not only Bing, but also Yahoo, DuckDuckGo, Copilot, and ChatGPT Search.

  • 1-Click GSC Import: Connect via your Google account to automatically import verified domain ownership and submitted sitemaps.
  • Bypassing the 48-Hour Sync Lag: GSC synchronization can take up to 48 hours. By clicking [Sitemaps] > [Submit sitemap] and manually entering https://globaldevlog.com/sitemap.xml (plus localized variants), Bing's crawler dispatches immediately.

5. Verification Checklist​

Before announcing your custom domain, run this sanity check:

  • DNS Resolution: globaldevlog.com and www.globaldevlog.com resolve without SSL warnings.
  • Canonical CNAME: static/CNAME deployed to GitHub Pages origin.
  • AdSense Assets: https://globaldevlog.com/ads.txt returns HTTP 200 with matching publisher ID.
  • Localized Sitemaps: All language sitemaps (/sitemap.xml, /ko/, /ja/, /es/) return HTTP 200.
  • Search Console Health: Google, Naver, and Bing show clean, verified properties with active RSS feeds.

With this modern infrastructure in place, your static blog operates with the speed of an edge CDN, zero server hosting bills, maximum search visibility across four languages, and full readiness for AdSense monetization.

item.title: From 45 npm Vulnerabilities to Zero-Risk: Why You Shouldn't Blindly Run npm audit fix --force on Static Sites
item.description: A deep dive into static site threat modeling, dissecting why 45 npm vulnerabilities in build tools pose zero runtime risk on GitHub Pages, and why running npm audit fix --force breaks production.
item.content:encoded:
Every modern frontend developer has experienced this sudden spike of adrenaline: you run npm audit on your clean documentation or blog repository, and the terminal screams back in alarming red text:

45 vulnerabilities (15 moderate, 15 high, 15 critical)
To address all issues (including breaking changes), run:
  npm audit fix --force

Seeing words like Critical, Remote Code Execution (RCE), and Prototype Pollution triggers an immediate instinct: type npm audit fix --force to make the scary red warnings go away.

However, in the world of Static Site Generators (SSG) like Docusaurus, Next.js, or Hugo deployed to GitHub Pages or AWS S3, doing so is often an engineering mistake that breaks production builds without improving your actual security posture.

In this article, we dissect the static site threat model, explain why bundler vulnerabilities differ fundamentally from server vulnerabilities, and share a production-tested 4-Layer Security Hardening Blueprint to protect what actually matters: your secrets, client privacy, and repository integrity.

1. Executive Summary: The Core Engineering Trade-off​

  1. Build-Time Tools != Production Runtime: Packages flagged in npm audit (such as tinypool, serialize-javascript, postcss-selector-parser) are node worker and bundler dependencies executed locally on your machine during npm run build.
  2. Zero Live Server on CDN: Once compiled, GitHub Pages serves static, immutable HTML, CSS, and client-side JavaScript. There is no running Node.js daemon, no backend port listening, and no database connection in production.
  3. The Danger of --force: Running npm audit fix --force blindly downgrades core frameworks (e.g., rolling Docusaurus back to older releases), breaking React 19 compatibility, MDX v3 pipelines, and future flag architectures.
  4. Where Real Static Risks Lie: The genuine security risks of static blogs are credential/API key leakage in public Git history, PII exposure in datasets, and client-side cross-origin leakage.

2. Anatomy of the 45 Vulnerabilities: Build vs Runtime​

Let's examine the actual CVEs reported in our audit log:

A. Tinypool Prototype Pollution (GHSA-5gmw-xhrv-c9v3 - Critical)​

  • Vulnerability: If untrusted user input is passed into the worker initialization options of tinypool, an attacker can pollute Object.prototype.
  • Reality in SSG: tinypool is used internally by @docusaurus/faster to parallelize bundling tasks across CPU cores during build time. The input parameters come solely from your own docusaurus.config.ts. No external visitor on your website can send HTTP payloads to your local CPU worker pool.

B. Serialize-JavaScript RCE (GHSA-5c6j-r48x-rmvq - High)​

  • Vulnerability: Remote Code Execution via crafted RegExp flags or serialized dates.
  • Reality in SSG: Webpack uses this to serialize internal compilation chunks into static .js bundles. Once written to the build/ directory, JavaScript files are passive assets served over HTTPS. No server-side deserialization takes place.

C. PostCSS Selector Parser CPU Exhaustion (GHSA-rj75-hqrm-r3gf - Moderate)​

  • Vulnerability: Quadratic complexity in flat selector parsing allows Denial of Service (DoS) via maliciously crafted CSS strings.
  • Reality in SSG: The CSS files being parsed are your own theme stylesheets (custom.css). Unless an attacker has write access to your Git repository, your build server will never parse untrusted external CSS.

Running npm audit fix --force in this situation attempts to downgrade @docusaurus/core from 3.10.2 to 3.7.0. This breaks Docusaurus v4 future flags and React 19 rendering, introducing breaking bugs into your codebase to patch an exploit that cannot physically occur in your architecture.

3. What Actually Matters: The 4-Layer Static Security Blueprint​

If npm bundler vulnerabilities are low risk, where should static site engineers invest their security budget? Here is the multi-layered defense pipeline implemented in this blog.

Layer 1: Automated Pre-Commit Secret Scanning​

The single greatest catastrophic risk for public technical blogs is accidentally committing an OpenAI key (sk-...), a GitHub Personal Access Token (ghp_...), or an AWS access credential (AKIA...).

We created an automated audit script (tools/audit_security.py) that utilizes Git's object database to scan every tracked file against high-entropy regex patterns:

PATTERNS = [
    (r'(?i)(api[_-]?key|secret|token|password|auth|bearer)\s*[:=]\s*["\']([^"\']{8,})["\']', "Potential Key Assignment"),
    (r'ghp_[a-zA-Z0-9]{36}', "GitHub Personal Access Token"),
    (r'sk-[a-zA-Z0-9]{32,}', "OpenAI API Key"),
    (r'AIzaSy[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{33}', "Google API Key"),
    (r'AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}', "AWS Access Key"),
    (r'-----BEGIN\s+(RSA\s+)?PRIVATE\s+KEY-----', "Private Key Certificate"),
]

Running this audit script before every release ensures zero hardcoded tokens ever reach the remote repository.

Layer 2: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) Scrubbing​

When publishing engineering articles on AI datasets (such as our 23-part Maeumjigi clinical counseling series or 5-part ANPR Vision AI series):

  • Synthetic Data First: All counseling records were synthetically generated via LLM pipelines (synth_gen) rather than using real clinical transcripts, guaranteeing zero medical privacy breach.
  • Regex PII Audit: Our scanner automatically validates markdown text against Korean national identity numbers (\d{6}-[1-4]\d{6}) and phone numbers (010-\d{4}-\d{4}).

Layer 3: Hardened .gitignore Configuration​

A standard .gitignore often ignores .env.local while leaving .env exposed. We hardened .gitignore to comprehensively block sensitive files, private certificates, and raw analytics dumps:

# Environment & Secret Protection
.env
.env.*
*.pem
*.key
*.pfx
*.cert
*credential*
*.secret

# Analytics & CSV dumps
*.csv

# Archived template files
_old/

Layer 4: Client-Side Privacy & Iframe Sandboxing​

Even without a backend server, static sites must respect user privacy and prevent data leakage:

  1. Strict Referrer Policy: In docusaurus.config.ts, we inject a strict referrer header into <head>:

    themeConfig: {
      metadata: [
        { name: 'referrer', content: 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin' },
      ],
    }

    This ensures that when a reader clicks an external documentation link, your blog's specific full URL parameters are truncated, preventing path leakage.

  2. Giscus Discussion Sandboxing: We host comments via GitHub Discussions. In BlogPostItem/index.tsx, Giscus is configured with:

    • emitMetadata="0": Prevents post-message iframe broadcasts from exposing discussion details to third-party browser scripts.
    • loading="lazy": Prevents iframe resource execution until the reader scrolls to the bottom of the article.

4. Key Takeaways for Developers​

  • Do Not Panic at npm audit: Always distinguish between Build-Time Bundler Dependencies and Production Runtime Dependencies.
  • Beware of --force: Automated downgrades often introduce real, breaking application bugs while solving theoretical vulnerabilities that cannot be triggered on a static CDN.
  • Focus on the Real Attack Surface: Automate secret detection, scrub sensitive data from datasets, enforce strict client-side referrer policies, and protect your Git history.

item.title: [Vision AI] Korean ANPR OCR Engine, Regex Normalization & Temporal Majority Voting (v01 to v11 Evolution) (#5)
item.description: Korean license plate syntax validation, EasyOCR tuning, temporal sliding window majority voting, and the complete 11-iteration engineering journey from v01 to v11.
item.content:encoded:
📌 Key Takeaways (TL;DR)

  • Problem: Single-frame OCR inevitably suffers from transient misreadings (e.g., 64아1511, 24가1511) due to vehicle yaw, glare, and vibration.
  • Solution: Implemented Korean plate regex validation (^\d{2,3}[가-힣]\d{4}$) coupled with a temporal sliding window majority voting engine across a 7-frame buffer (plate_confirm_threshold=3).
  • Result: Advanced through 11 system iterations (v01 to v11), transitioning from initial gibberish (ACCIIXOY-1Z01...) on June 5 to deterministic confirmation of 64가1511 on June 7 with 99.4% reliability.

1. Korean ANPR Syntax & EasyOCR Tuning​

Korean vehicle registration plates follow strict regulatory syntax:

Syntax: [2 or 3 Digits] + [1 Hangul Syllable] + [4 Digits]
Example: 64가1511, 123가4567
import easyocr
import re
from collections import deque, Counter

reader = easyocr.Reader(['ko', 'en'], gpu=True)

def parse_korean_plate(plate_img):
    results = reader.readtext(plate_img, detail=0)
    raw_text = "".join(results).replace(" ", "")
    
    # Korean License Plate Regex Match
    pattern = r'(\d{2,3}[가-힣]\d{4})'
    match = re.search(pattern, raw_text)
    return match.group(1) if match else None

2. Temporal Majority Voting Engine​

To overcome transient single-frame OCR flicker, we maintain a sliding history queue:

plate_history = deque(maxlen=CONFIG["plate_history_size"])  # 7
confirmed_plate = None

def update_plate_voting(detected_text):
    global confirmed_plate
    if detected_text:
        plate_history.append(detected_text)
        
    if len(plate_history) >= CONFIG["plate_confirm_threshold"]:
        counts = Counter(plate_history)
        most_common_plate, count = counts.most_common(1)[0]
        
        # Confirm plate if 3 or more votes agree
        if count >= CONFIG["plate_confirm_threshold"]:
            confirmed_plate = most_common_plate
            
    return confirmed_plate

item.title: [Vision AI] Overcoming Blurry Blackbox Artifacts: Deep Super-Resolution (EDSR vs FSRCNN) & Multi-Frame Image Stacking (#4)
item.description: Reconstructing cropped low-resolution license plate patches via EDSR 4x deep super-resolution and temporal multi-frame image stacking.
item.content:encoded:
📌 Key Takeaways (TL;DR)

  • Problem: Cropped license plates from dashcam footage often measure under 40x20 pixels with heavy H.264 macroblocking; standard bicubic interpolation fails to resolve character contours.
  • Solution: Integrated EDSR_x4 deep residual networks (EDSR_x4.pb) that omit batch normalization to preserve dynamic range, combined with temporal multi-frame image stacking across 3 to 5 consecutive frames.
  • Result: Quadrupled plate pixel density and sharpened stroke edges, lifting downstream EasyOCR accuracy on Korean characters from 32% to over 91%.

1. Resolution Limitations & The Need for Deep Super-Resolution​

Even with precise license plate localization, optical limitations thwart standard OCR:

  1. Failure of Bicubic Scaling: Interpolation algorithms blur edges further without hallucinating high-frequency contours.
  2. H.264 Compression & Sensor Noise: Dashcam compression creates severe pixelation that distorts alphanumeric strokes.

We integrated EDSR_x4 via the OpenCV DNN Super-Resolution module to reconstruct high-frequency details:

import cv2
from cv2 import dnn_superres

def init_super_resolution_engine(model_path="EDSR_x4.pb"):
    sr = dnn_superres.DnnSuperResImpl_create()
    sr.readModel(model_path)
    sr.setModel("edsr", 4)
    sr.setPreferableBackend(cv2.dnn.DNN_BACKEND_CUDA)
    sr.setPreferableTarget(cv2.dnn.DNN_TARGET_CUDA)
    return sr

2. Multi-Frame Image Stacking for Noise Reduction​

I_stacked(x, y) = (1 / N) * Σ Warp(I_i(x, y))

This temporal stacking cancels random sensor noise while boosting text-background contrast.

item.title: [Vision AI] Hierarchical Object Detection: YOLOv3 Vehicle ROI, YOLOv5 Plate Detector & CSRT Tracking (#3)
item.description: Two-stage hierarchical localization: broad vehicle detection via YOLOv3, localized license plate inference via YOLOv5, and CSRT correlation filter tracking.
item.content:encoded:
📌 Key Takeaways (TL;DR)

  • Problem: Searching for tiny plates (30x15 pixels) across the raw 640x480 frame generates massive false positives from roadside signs and drops inference speed below 10 FPS.
  • Solution: Designed a two-stage hierarchical architecture: broad vehicle detection (YOLOv3-tiny) crops the vehicle ROI, within which a fine-tuned YOLOv5 (lp_det.pt, conf=0.6) locates the license plate. Integrated OpenCV CSRT correlation filter tracking with a 15-frame redetection interval.
  • Result: Eliminated 98% of background false positives and slashed GPU overhead by 80%, sustaining real-time 50+ FPS continuous tracking.

1. The Pitfalls of Global Detection & The Hierarchical Solution​

Running plate detectors across the full 640x480 image causes two critical flaws:

  1. Background Clutter: Street advertisements, road billboards, and store signs trigger high false-alarm rates.
  2. Resolution Downsampling Loss: Resizing 640x480 to typical model inputs (e.g., 640x640) squashes tiny 30-pixel plates into sub-feature extinction.

Our two-stage hierarchical pipeline addresses this by constraining the search space:

vehicle_boxes = detect_vehicles_yolov3(frame, net=vehicle_net, conf_thresh=0.5)

for box in vehicle_boxes:
    x1, y1, x2, y2 = box
    vehicle_roi = frame[y1:y2, x1:x2]
    plate_boxes = plate_model(vehicle_roi)
    for pbox in plate_boxes:
        px1, py1, px2, py2 = pbox
        global_plate_box = [x1 + px1, y1 + py1, x1 + px2, y1 + py2]

2. Real-Time Latency Mitigation: CSRT Tracker Integration​

if frame_count % CONFIG["detection_interval"] == 0:
    boxes = detect_vehicles_yolov3(frame)
    tracker = cv2.TrackerCSRT_create()
    tracker.init(frame, tuple(boxes[0]))
else:
    success, tracked_box = tracker.update(frame)
    if not success:
        tracker = None

item.title: [Vision AI] Dynamic Lane Boundary Extraction & Geometric IoU Intrusion Criterion (#2)
item.description: Canny edge filtering, probabilistic Hough transform (HoughLinesP), slope thresholding, and geometric polygon IoU intrusion calculation.
item.content:encoded:
📌 Key Takeaways (TL;DR)

  • Problem: Dashcam footage contains heavy pavement specular reflection, tar cracks, and road shadows that induce false lane lines; simple coordinate checking cannot reliably catch the exact moment of lane encroachment.
  • Solution: Implemented vanishing-point trapezoidal ROI masking, slope thresholding (|slope| > 0.5), and a 7-frame temporal moving average queue. Formulated intrusion as geometric IoU between vehicle tire footprints and lane boundaries.
  • Result: Filtered out >95% of road texture noise while capturing vehicle lane crossing events with sub-frame accuracy.

1. Dynamic Lane Detection: Canny & Probabilistic Hough Transform​

def detect_lanes(frame):
    height, width = frame.shape[:2]
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    blur = cv2.GaussianBlur(gray, (5, 5), 0)
    edges = cv2.Canny(blur, 50, 150)
    
    mask = np.zeros_like(edges)
    roi_polygon = np.array([[
        (int(width * 0.1), height),
        (int(width * 0.45), int(height * 0.6)),
        (int(width * 0.55), int(height * 0.6)),
        (int(width * 0.9), height)
    ]], np.int32)
    cv2.fillPoly(mask, roi_polygon, 255)
    masked_edges = cv2.bitwise_and(edges, mask)
    
    lines = cv2.HoughLinesP(
        masked_edges,
        rho=1,
        theta=np.pi / 180,
        threshold=20,
        minLineLength=20,
        maxLineGap=10
    )
    return lines

2. Slope Filtering & Temporal Smoothing​

Raw line segments are filtered using slope criteria:

Slope m = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1)
  • Left Lane: m < -0.5
  • Right Lane: m > 0.5
  • Horizontal Noise: |m| <= 0.5 (crosswalks and bumps are rejected)

A deque(maxlen=7) temporal moving average smooths lane equations across consecutive frames.

3. Geometric Polygon IoU Lane Intrusion Criterion​

Footprint = [x_min, y_min + 0.7*h, x_max, y_max]
IoU = Area(Footprint ∩ Lane_Polygon) / Area(Footprint)
def check_lane_intrusion(vehicle_box, lane_polygon, threshold=0.05):
    vx1, vy1, vx2, vy2 = vehicle_box
    vh = vy2 - vy1
    footprint = Polygon([(vx1, vy1 + 0.7*vh), (vx2, vy1 + 0.7*vh), (vx2, vy2), (vx1, vy2)])
    
    intersection = footprint.intersection(lane_polygon).area
    iou = intersection / footprint.area
    return iou > threshold, iou

When IoU > 0.05, the system flags a violation event and triggers YOLOv5 license plate localization.

item.title: [Vision AI] Blackbox Lane Intrusion & Super-Resolution ANPR: 6-Stage End-to-End Pipeline & Real-Time Constraints (#1)
item.description: Architecting a 6-stage computer vision pipeline combining dynamic lane detection, IoU intrusion metrics, YOLOv5 license plate detection, EDSR super-resolution, and OCR voting.
item.content:encoded:
📌 Key Takeaways (TL;DR)

  • Problem: Low-resolution dashcam footage suffers from severe vehicle vibration, nighttime backlighting, and heavy motion blur, making direct license plate recognition and lane violation tracking extremely error-prone.
  • Solution: Designed a unified 6-stage vision architecture: Canny/Hough lane extraction -> YOLOv3 vehicle detection -> polygon IoU lane violation calculation -> YOLOv5 plate localization -> EDSR_x4 super-resolution -> EasyOCR temporal voting.
  • Result: Constructed an end-to-end Python pipeline achieving robust vehicle tracking and lane boundary monitoring even under degraded dashcam conditions.

1. Project Background: Why Dashcam Vision is Hard​

In intelligent transportation systems (ITS) and autonomous traffic enforcement, real-time lane intrusion detection and automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) are foundational capabilities. However, real-world dashcam footage presents severe optical challenges:

  1. Extreme Low Resolution & Blurred Textures: The license plate of a leading or overtaking vehicle often spans merely 30x15 to 50x25 pixels across a 640x480 frame, causing alphanumeric strokes to merge into indistinct blobs.
  2. Vehicle Vibration & Rolling Shutter Distortions: Road bumps, sudden decelerations, and perspective shifts distort straight lane boundaries.
  3. Real-Time Latency Bottlenecks: Executing heavy full-frame vision transformers per frame results in fatal FPS drops, disabling real-time tracking.

2. 6-Stage Hierarchical Pipeline Architecture​

To achieve both high precision and high throughput, we modularized the system into a 6-stage decoupled pipeline:

flowchart TD
    Raw["Raw Dashcam Frame 640x480"] --> L1["Stage 1: Canny + Hough Dynamic Lane Extraction"]
    Raw --> L2["Stage 2: YOLOv3-tiny Vehicle Detection"]
    L1 & L2 --> L3["Stage 3: Vehicle Footprint & Lane Polygon IoU Intrusion Metric"]
    L3 -- If Intrusion Triggered --> L4["Stage 4: Localized YOLOv5 Plate Detection in Vehicle ROI"]
    L4 --> L5["Stage 5: EDSR_x4 Deep 4x Super-Resolution"]
    L5 --> L6["Stage 6: EasyOCR + Regex + Temporal Majority Voting"]
    L6 --> Result["Confirmed Violation Plate: 64가1511"]

Decoupled Processing Responsibilities​

  1. Lane Extraction: Trapezoidal dynamic ROI masking, Canny edge detection, and slope filtering isolate driving corridor bounds.
  2. Vehicle Detection: Lightweight YOLOv3-tiny outputs candidate vehicle bounding boxes in milliseconds.
  3. Intrusion Criterion: Computes geometric Intersection-over-Union (IoU > 0.05) between vehicle tire footprint and the lane boundary polygon.
  4. Plate Localization: YOLOv5 (lp_det.pt) evaluates only the cropped vehicle ROI, saving immense compute cycles.
  5. Super-Resolution: The cropped plate patch is passed through a deep EDSR_x4 neural network, reconstructing high-frequency character contours.
  6. OCR & Majority Voting: EasyOCR extracts alphanumeric tokens, which undergo Korean syntax regex validation and temporal multi-frame voting to confirm the plate number.

3. Core System Parameters (CONFIG)​

}

item.title: [Webots Robotics] Sim-to-Real: Hardware Transfer via Arduino Uno, HC-06 Bluetooth & ArUco Vision Tracking (#5)
item.description: Deploying the simulation-trained 648-bin Q-Learning policy onto a physical 2-wheeled Arduino Uno robot using ceiling webcam homography and real-time ArUco 6-DoF marker pose tracking.
item.content:encoded:
📌 Key Takeaways (TL;DR)

  • Problem: Severe computational constraints on microcontrollers (Arduino Uno ATmega328P with only 2KB SRAM), non-linear wheel slip, noisy ultrasonic sensing, and the classical Reality Gap between Webots simulation physics and physical hardware.
  • Solution: Designed a distributed I/O architecture (HC-06 Bluetooth at 115,200 baud) where a host PC runs OpenCV vision processing and Q-Table inference while the Arduino handles low-level PWM motor actuation. Overhead camera lens distortion correction and ArUco marker homography (vision.py) deliver sub-centimeter real-time (x, y, θ) tracking.
  • Result: Zero-shot transfer of the simulation-trained 648-state Q-Table achieved an 86.7% target reaching success rate (26/30 trials) in a physical 1.2m × 1.2m arena, successfully closing the reality gap without real-world fine-tuning.

1. The Challenge of Sim-to-Real: Navigating the Reality Gap​

In virtual Webots simulations, surface friction coefficients remain idealized, wheel motors rotate with deterministic precision, and simulated distance sensors yield noiseless measurements. Real hardware, however, introduces unpredictable physical perturbations:

  1. Severe Memory & Compute Bottlenecks: The Arduino Uno (ATmega328P) operates with only 32KB flash memory and 2KB SRAM. Running deep neural networks or heavy matrix operations directly on-chip is physically impossible.
  2. Sensor Noise & Blind Angles: Inexpensive ultrasonic rangefinders suffer from specular reflection at shallow incidence angles, reporting 0 or spiking to maximum range when pinging smooth acrylic boundaries.
  3. Wheel Slip & Odometry Drift: Minor variations in wheel friction and motor gearboxes cause differential-drive robots to veer off-course even when commanded to drive straight, making dead-reckoning odometry completely unreliable.

2. Distributed Control Architecture: Host PC (Brain) ↔ Arduino (Muscle)​

To overcome microcontroller limitations, we decoupled high-level reasoning from low-level actuation: "PC as the brain, Arduino as the muscle."

flowchart TD
    subgraph CeilingCam["Ceiling Vision System (Overhead Camera)"]
        Cam["FHD Webcam (30 FPS)"]
        Aruco["ArUco Marker Detection (DICT_4X4_50)<br>Perspective Homography (homography.npy)"]
        Cam --> Aruco
    end

    subgraph PC["Host PC (Python Engine)"]
        Pose["Robot Pose Estimation (x, y, θ)"]
        Disc["648-bin Discretizer"]
        QL["Trained Q-Table (ε=0)"]
        BT_Host["HC-06 Bluetooth SPP (115200 baud)"]
        
        Aruco --> Pose --> Disc --> QL --> BT_Host
    end

    subgraph Robot["Physical Mobile Robot (Real Hardware)"]
        BT_Slave["HC-06 Bluetooth Receiver"]
        MCU["Arduino Uno (Firmware)"]
        Motors["L298N Dual H-Bridge + Geared DC Motors"]
        
        BT_Host <-->|"Action Byte [0..3]<br>Ack/Status"| BT_Slave --> MCU --> Motors
    end
  • Host PC Pipeline: An overhead webcam captures the complete arena top-down, tracking an ArUco fiducial marker mounted on top of the robot at 30 FPS. The robot's planar pose (x, y, θ) is calculated and mapped into the discrete 648-state space to retrieve the optimal greedy action from the Q-Table.
  • HC-06 Serial Communication: To minimize Round-Trip Time (RTT) over the Bluetooth Serial Port Profile (SPP), the transmission baud rate was upgraded from the default 9,600 to 115,200 bps, sustaining a low-latency 30~50Hz control loop.
  • Arduino Firmware (arduino_firmware.ino): Upon receiving single-byte action commands (0: Forward, 1: Backward, 2: Turn Left, 3: Turn Right), the microcontroller modulates PWM pins on the L298N motor driver for precise tick-based open-loop pulses.

3. Overhead Camera Homography & ArUco Vision Tracking​

To measure robot positioning and obstacle proximity with millimeter accuracy across the real arena, we built an OpenCV-based top-down computer vision pipeline.

📐 Perspective Rectification & Homography (calib_auto.py)​

  1. Checkerboard Distortion Calibration: To eliminate barrel distortion from wide-angle webcam lenses, intrinsic camera matrix (K) and distortion coefficients (D) were pre-computed using a standard 9×6 checkerboard.
  2. Perspective Homography: To project the angled camera viewpoint into a canonical 1.2m × 1.2m square bird's-eye view, a 3×3 perspective homography matrix (homography.npy) was established from the 4 marked arena corner coordinates.

💻 ArUco Marker Pose Tracking Implementation (vision.py)​

import cv2
import numpy as np

# Load ArUco dictionary and detection parameters
aruco_dict = cv2.aruco.getPredefinedDictionary(cv2.aruco.DICT_4X4_50)
parameters = cv2.aruco.DetectorParameters()
detector = cv2.aruco.ArucoDetector(aruco_dict, parameters)

def get_robot_pose(frame, homography_matrix):
    """Calculates planar coordinates (x, y) and heading angle (theta) from rectified image."""
    warped = cv2.warpPerspective(frame, homography_matrix, (600, 600))
    corners, ids, _ = detector.detectMarkers(warped)
    
    if ids is not None and len(ids) > 0:
        c = corners[0][0]
        center_x = float(np.mean(c[:, 0]))
        center_y = float(np.mean(c[:, 1]))
        
        # Calculate heading angle (theta) from marker front edge vector
        front_x = (c[0][0] + c[1][0]) / 2.0
        front_y = (c[0][1] + c[1][1]) / 2.0
        theta = np.arctan2(front_y - center_y, front_x - center_x)
        
        return center_x, center_y, theta
    return None

4. Hardware Troubleshooting & Real-World Deployment Results​

Transitioning from simulation to physical operation revealed critical edge cases addressed through robust engineering countermeasures:

Symptom (Troubleshooting)Root CauseEngineering Solution
Robot drifts sideways during forward commandGearbox friction differences between left & right DC motorsImplemented an interactive calibration script (ble_vision_turn_calib.py) to apply dynamic PWM trim offsets
Runaway behavior during Bluetooth disconnectPacket drops under RF interference causing robot to retain last commandEmbedded a 200ms communication watchdog timer in firmware to immediately cut motor power upon signal loss
Intermittent ArUco marker detection lossSpecular glare from ceiling fluorescent lighting on glossy marker surfaceFine-tuned adaptive thresholding parameters and added a 1D Kalman Filter position extrapolator

🏆 Final Real-World Benchmark​

  • Autonomous Goal Reaching Rate: Tested across 30 independent trials in the physical 1.2m × 1.2m obstacle arena, the robot achieved an 86.7% success rate (26/30 successful arrivals).
  • Leveraging just 2,592 pre-computed discrete Q-values (~2.5 KB), the agent navigated complex physical obstacles without any real-world gradient updates.

5. Concluding the RL Q-Learning Dev Log Series​

With this final Sim-to-Real deployment, our 5-part RL Q-Learning Robotics series reaches its conclusion:

  1. #1: 648-Bin State Discretization & Webots TCP Socket IPC Architecture
  2. #2: Tabular Q-Learning ε-Decay Exploration & Multi-Objective Reward Shaping
  3. #3: Overcoming Arena Local Minima in 12-Wall Environments via Headless Pipelines
  4. #4: Quantitative Benchmark with evaluate_qlearning vs. SARSA & DQN
  5. #5: Sim-to-Real Hardware Transfer via Arduino Uno, Bluetooth SPP & ArUco Vision

From foundational simulator modeling and algorithmic tuning to multi-seed automation and physical hardware deployment, this series documented the complete lifecycle of reinforcement learning for embedded robotics. Stay tuned for future deep dives into our next projects!

item.title: [Webots Robotics] Deterministic Evaluation via evaluate_qlearning & Benchmark vs. DQN and SARSA (#4)
item.description: Zero-exploration (ε=0) deterministic evaluation pipeline with evaluate_qlearning.py, examining path efficiency, near-miss metrics, and benchmark comparisons against DQN and SARSA.
item.content:encoded:
📌 Key Takeaways (TL;DR)

  • Objective: Measure the pure, deterministic performance of the learned greedy policy (ε=0) without exploration noise, validating real-world deployability.
  • Methodology: Implemented evaluate_qlearning.py running 30 independent trials across 5 round-robin evaluation seeds, rigorously tracking success rates, path efficiency vs. theoretical shortest routes, and obstacle near-miss counts.
  • Result: Tabular Q-Learning attained a 93.3% deterministic success rate in the 12-wall arena with superior path smoothness and ultra-low 0.02ms inference latency, outperforming heavier DQN and SARSA baselines.

1. Quantitative Evaluation Pipeline (evaluate_qlearning.py)​

Training reward curves are inherently noisy due to ε-greedy exploration. To evaluate the true deployment capability of our agent, we must test the purely deterministic policy ($\epsilon = 0$).

We built an evaluation runner that loads the saved Q-table (qlearning_qtable.npy) and evaluates the agent across 5 distinct test seeds (EVAL_SEEDS = (0, 1, 2, 3, 4)).

flowchart LR
    Model["Trained Q-Table<br>(qlearning_qtable.npy)"] --> Agent["Greedy Agent<br>(ε = 0 Fixed)"]
    EvalSeeds["5 Test Seeds<br>(EVAL_SEEDS 0..4)"] --> Webots["Webots Simulator<br>(30 Evaluation Trials)"]
    Agent <--> Webots
    Webots --> CSV["Trace & Metric Logging<br>(eval_log.csv / traces)"]

💻 Evaluation Loop Architecture​

# evaluate_qlearning.py excerpt
agent = QLearningAgent(seed=0)
agent.load(model_path) # Load trained Q-Table

for ep in range(n_episodes):
    env_seed = EVAL_SEEDS[ep % len(EVAL_SEEDS)]
    raw, info = env.reset(seed=env_seed, return_info=True)
    s = discretize(raw)
    
    for t in range(1, max_steps + 1):
        a = agent.act(s, deterministic=True) # Pure argmax Q(s, a)
        raw_next, r, done, info = env.step(a)
        s = discretize(raw_next)
        
        # Log trajectory coordinates and near-misses (dist <= 0.15m)
        record_metrics(info)
        if done: break

2. Comprehensive Evaluation Metrics​

  1. Success Rate: Percentage of runs reaching the target radius (0.10m) within 150 steps without collision.
  2. Path Efficiency: Ratio of theoretical shortest path distance (L_shortest) to actual traversed path length (L_actual). Path Efficiency (%) = (Shortest Path / Actual Path) × 100%
  3. Near-Miss Frequency: Number of steps where obstacle distance dipped below 0.15m.
  4. Oscillation Count: Metric penalizing back-and-forth steering jitter.

3. Algorithm Benchmark: Tabular Q-Learning vs. SARSA vs. DQN​

Comparative evaluation in the identical Webots 12-wall arena across the three reinforcement learning algorithms revealed clear performance trade-offs:

MetricTabular Q-Learning (Ours)SARSA (On-policy)Deep Q-Network (DQN)
Learning ParadigmOff-policy TD(0)On-policy TD(0)Neural Network (Deep RL)
Parameter Size2,592 floats (~2.5 KB)2,592 floats (~2.5 KB)~150,000 weights (~600 KB)
Deterministic Success Rate (obstacle12)93.3%86.7%90.0%
Average Steps per Episode41.2 steps48.5 steps44.7 steps
Per-Step Inference Latency0.02 ms (NumPy array lookup)0.02 ms2.15 ms (PyTorch forward pass)
Near-Miss FrequencyLow (balanced detour)Minimal (excessively conservative)Moderate

🔍 In-Depth Behavioral Analysis​

  • Why Q-Learning Excels: By evaluating max_a' Q(s', a'), off-policy Q-Learning ignores transient exploratory collisions during training, settling on the shortest feasible detour path.
  • SARSA's Conservative Bias: On-policy updates factor in exploration penalties, causing SARSA to over-correct and choose excessively long, inefficient detours to avoid walls at all costs.
  • DQN's Trade-off: DQN handles continuous inputs well, but training stability requires replay buffers and target networks, while its 2.15ms latency and GPU requirement impose severe constraints on lightweight microcontrollers like Arduino.

4. Evaluation Takeaways​

Our discrete 648-bin Tabular Q-Learning model requires just 2.5 KB of memory, yet matched and exceeded deep neural network models in success rate (93.3%) and real-time execution speed.

5. What's Next?​

With simulation benchmarks thoroughly concluded, the ultimate milestone remains: transferring policy to reality (Sim-to-Real).

In our final Episode #5, we will detail the hardware integration: deploying our policy to a 2-wheel differential Arduino Uno robot, communicating via HC-06 Bluetooth, and tracking ground-truth position via ceiling webcam checkerboard calibration and ArUco markers!

item.title: [Webots Robotics] Conquering Local Minima in 12-Wall Obstacles: Multi-Seed Headless Simulation (#3)
item.description: Overcoming the Local Minima dilemma in complex 12-wall obstacle environments (obstacle12) and orchestrating high-speed automated multi-seed Webots simulations.
item.content:encoded:
📌 Key Takeaways (TL;DR)

  • Problem: When a goal lies directly behind an obstacle, the myopic nature of distance-delta rewards (+0.1 × Δdist) pulls the robot into head-on collisions, trapping it in severe Local Minima.
  • Solution: Integrated 3-way head-scan obstacle perception (front/left/right) with long-horizon Bellman value propagation (γ=0.99), alongside an automated PowerShell Webots Headless pipeline (headless_run.ps1) executing multi-seed training across seeds 0, 1, and 2.
  • Result: The agent successfully learned robust detour policies in the 12-wall arena, achieving a 90%+ goal success rate after 600 episodes.

1. The Obstacle Challenge: The Local Minima Trap​

In an empty arena (no_obstacle), navigating is simply a matter of steering toward the target heading. However, introducing 12 interior walls (obstacle12) unveiled a critical bottleneck in reward design:

flowchart TD
    Start["Start (Robot)"]
    Wall["Obstacle Wall"]
    Goal["Target Goal"]
    
    Start -->|"Direct drive (greedy distance reward)"| Wall
    Wall -.->|"Collision & deadlocked (Local Minima)"| Wall
    Start ==>|"Detour Policy<br>Accepts temporary distance penalty"| Goal
  • The Dilemma: When the target is directly on the other side of an interior wall, driving straight ahead leads directly to collision.
  • Reward Conflict: Circumnavigating the wall requires moving temporarily away from the goal (negative distance delta). Under naive exploration, the agent enters a deadlock—spinning or timing out against the wall.

2. Solution Strategy: Head-Scan Perception & Value Backpropagation​

Overcoming this trap relies on coupling 3-directional head-scan perception with a high discount factor (γ = 0.99):

  1. Perceptual State Discretization:
    • Attempting to advance while front_distance = Danger yields a heavy collision penalty (-1.0).
    • Sweeping the sensor head left and right reveals free avenues (left_distance = Safe or right_distance = Safe), encouraging lateral turns.
  2. Long-Term Temporal Difference Credit Assignment:
    • Although turning away temporarily depresses the step reward, successfully rounding the wall and reaching the target yields the substantial terminal reward (+1.0).
    • Backpropagated through Q(s, a) with γ = 0.99, the agent gradually learns that detour steps possess higher expected return than head-on approaches.

3. Webots Headless Automation Pipeline​

Rigorous reinforcement learning requires multi-seed validation (Seeds 0, 1, 2). Running 1,500 episodes interactively in the Webots GUI three times would take many hours.

We automated this with a headless_run.ps1 PowerShell script, launching Webots in high-speed, no-render mode (--mode=fast --no-rendering):

💻 Automated Pipeline (headless_run.ps1)​

# Launch Webots in background headless fast mode
$webotsProc = Start-Process -FilePath $WebotsExe `
    -ArgumentList @("--mode=fast", "--no-rendering", "--stdout", "--stderr", $WorldFile) `
    -PassThru

# Train agent over socket IPC
python train_qlearning.py --scenario obstacle12 --seed 0 --episodes 1500

# Cleanup process and generate performance plots
Stop-Process -Id $webotsProc.Id -Force
python -m qlearning.plot_curves --log-dir logs/obstacle12/seed_0

4. Empirical Evaluation: Cross-Environment Learning Curves​

The graph above contrasts convergence across 3 random seeds between the unobstructed world (no_obstacle) and the 12-wall obstacle world (obstacle12).

📊 Benchmark Metrics​

MetricEmpty Arena (no_obstacle)12-Wall Arena (obstacle12)
Initial Convergence~300 - 400 episodes~600 - 800 episodes
Final Success Rate (100-ep MA)98.5% - 99.2%91.4% - 94.8%
Mean Steps per Episode15 - 22 steps38 - 52 steps (detour path)
Cross-Seed VarianceNegligible (highly stable)Moderate (exploration path dependency)
  • Extended Exploration: In obstacle12, discovering viable detour corridors requires approximately 200 additional episodes of random trials, keeping the average reward depressed until episode 400.
  • Detour Mastery: Beyond episode 800, all seeds stabilize above 90% success, confirming that the agent reliably maneuvers through tight gaps without collisions.

5. What's Next?​

Our 648-bin Tabular Q-Learning model successfully navigates maze-like obstacle configurations.

In Episode #4, we will load the saved model checkpoints (models/*.npy) to benchmark greedy, deterministic performance using evaluate_qlearning.py and analyze comparative metrics against DQN and SARSA!

item.title: [Webots Robotics] Tabular Q-Learning Implementation & Reward Shaping Tuning (#2)
item.description: In-depth breakdown of Tabular Q-Learning TD(0) update formulas, exponential epsilon-decay exploration, and dense reward shaping to overcome sparse rewards in mobile robot navigation.
item.content:encoded:
📌 Key Takeaways (TL;DR)

  • Problem: Sparse reward setups (+1.0 at goal, -1.0 at collision) cause severe exploration delays, causing the agent to wander or spin for thousands of episodes before stumbling upon the target.
  • Solution: Implemented a multi-objective Dense Reward Shaping mechanism combining potential-based Euclidean distance delta rewards (+0.1 × Δdist) with step (-0.01), turning (-0.01), and backward (-0.05) penalties, paired with exponential epsilon decay (1.0 → 0.05).
  • Result: The moving average reward shifted into a steady positive regime (0.7+) within 500 episodes in the no_obstacle scenario, achieving a 98%+ goal success rate.

1. Tabular Q-Learning Update Formula & Agent Architecture​

Tabular Q-Learning is an off-policy Temporal Difference (TD(0)) algorithm grounded in the Bellman Optimality Equation.

The agent maintains an action-value table Q(s, a) structured as a 2D NumPy array of shape $(648, 4)$. Using the experience transition tuple $(s, a, r, s', done)$ streamed from the Webots socket server, the $Q$-values are updated in real time via:

📐 Q-Learning TD(0) Update Rule​

Target = r + γ * max_a' Q(s', a') * (1 - done)
TD Error = Target - Q(s, a)
Q(s, a) <- Q(s, a) + α * TD Error
  • Learning Rate (α = 0.1): Balances the rate of incorporating new feedback versus retaining historical estimates.
  • Discount Factor (γ = 0.99): Values long-term future returns, critical for multi-step navigation.
  • Terminal Masking (1 - done): Clamps future expectations to zero upon goal arrival or collision, isolating the terminal reward.

💻 Agent Core Implementation (qlearning_agent.py)​

import numpy as np

class QLearningAgent:
    def __init__(self, n_states=648, n_actions=4, alpha=0.1, gamma=0.99,
                 eps_start=1.0, eps_min=0.05, eps_decay=0.995, seed=0):
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        self.Q = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions), dtype=np.float64)
        self.alpha = float(alpha)
        self.gamma = float(gamma)
        self.epsilon = float(eps_start)
        self.eps_min = float(eps_min)
        self.eps_decay = float(eps_decay)
        self.n_actions = int(n_actions)

    def act(self, s: int, deterministic: bool = False) -> int:
        """ε-Greedy behavior policy: Exploration vs. Exploitation"""
        if (not deterministic) and self.rng.random() < self.epsilon:
            return int(self.rng.integers(self.n_actions))
        return int(np.argmax(self.Q[s]))

    def update(self, s: int, a: int, r: float, s_next: int, done: bool) -> float:
        """TD(0) Off-policy Q-Table update"""
        target = r if done else r + self.gamma * float(np.max(self.Q[s_next]))
        td_error = target - self.Q[s, a]
        self.Q[s, a] += self.alpha * td_error
        return float(td_error)

    def decay_epsilon(self):
        """Exponential decay executed at the end of each episode"""
        self.epsilon = max(self.eps_min, self.epsilon * self.eps_decay)

2. Exponential Epsilon-Greedy Decay Strategy​

At the start of training, the agent has zero domain knowledge, requiring ε = 1.0 (100% random exploration) to discover the arena boundaries.

However, an uncurbed exploration rate induces perpetual collisions even after the optimal path has been resolved. We apply per-episode exponential decay:

ε_(ep+1) = max(ε_min, ε_ep × 0.995)

  • Episode 1: ε = 1.0 (Full exploration)
  • Episode 300: ε ≈ 0.22 (Shift toward exploiting high Q-values)
  • Episode 600: ε = 0.05 (Floor exploration rate ε_min, 95% greedy execution)

3. Dense Reward Shaping for Sparse Navigation​

A fundamental challenge in mobile robotics is sparse reward feedback. In a 1.2m × 1.2m arena, moving randomly yields zero reward until the robot coincidentally intersects the $0.10m$ goal tolerance.

To guide convergence, we engineered a Dense Reward Shaping schedule inside the Webots controller (RL_controller.py):

Reward ComponentValueDesign Objective & Physical Effect
Goal Reached (REWARD_GOAL)+1.0Terminal reward on successful target arrival
Wall/Obstacle Collision (REWARD_COLLISION)-1.0Severe penalty on physical impact
Distance Delta Reward (REWARD_DELTA_SCALE)+0.1 × ΔdistImmediate feedback proportional to Euclidean distance reduction
Step Time Penalty (REWARD_STEP)-0.01Prevents idling and incentivizes shortest paths
Turning Penalty (REWARD_TURN)-0.01Suppresses unproductive spinning behavior
Backward Penalty (REWARD_BACKWARD)-0.05Discourages inefficient reverse driving

🔍 Mathematical Principle of Distance Delta​

Δdist = dist_prev - dist_curr

  • Driving $0.05m$ toward the target awards $+0.1 \times 0.05 = +0.005$ immediately.
  • Conversely, driving away incurs an instant penalty, allowing the agent to align its heading with the target within the first 100 episodes.

4. Empirical Evaluation: Reward and Success Curves​

Training for 1,500 episodes in the no_obstacle world demonstrated remarkable convergence matching our theoretical expectations.

📈 Convergence Milestones​

  1. Episodes 0 ~ 200 (Exploration Phase):
    • Frequent wall collisions and 150-step timeouts keep the moving average reward in the negative range (-0.4 ~ -0.2).
  2. Episodes 200 ~ 500 (Ascent Phase):
    • As distance-delta rewards propagate through the Q-Table, the policy establishes a strong forward-driving preference whenever goal_heading is centered.
    • Success rate surges from 20% to over 80%.
  3. Episodes 500 ~ 1,500 (Asymptotic Convergence):
    • With ε settled at 0.05, average steps per episode plummet from 150 (timeout) to 15 ~ 22 steps.
    • The 100-episode moving average success rate converges above 98.5%.

5. What's Next?​

We have proven that Tabular Q-Learning over 648 states solves empty arena navigation cleanly.

However, real-world environments are packed with walls and obstacles. In Episode #3, we will investigate the obstacle12 and obstacle_hard maps, examining how our agent handles local minima traps and running multi-seed parallel training!

item.title: [Webots Robotics] Q-Learning Autonomous Navigation: 648-Bin State Discretization & Socket Architecture (#1)
item.description: Designing a 648-bin state space discretizer and a TCP socket IPC architecture for Webots mobile robot autonomous navigation with tabular Q-Learning.
item.content:encoded:
📌 Key Takeaways (TL;DR)

  • Problem: Continuous sensor readings (distance & heading) cause a state-space explosion for tabular Q-learning, and synchronous IPC with the Webots simulator requires low-latency coordination.
  • Solution: Designed a geometrically partitioned 5-dimensional continuous sensor mapper producing 3 × 8 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 648 discrete states (discretizer.py) and a line-delimited JSON IPC socket pipeline over TCP port 5000.
  • Result: Achieved O(1) fast Q-Table indexing and reliable 32ms physics synchronization between the simulator and Python agent.

1. Project Background: Why Webots and Q-Learning?​

Enabling an autonomous differential-drive robot to navigate an unknown indoor arena and reach a target while avoiding obstacles is a foundational robotics challenge. While Deep Reinforcement Learning (DQN, PPO) handles complex inputs, it demands high computational overhead and lacks straightforward interpretability.

In this project, we apply classical Tabular Q-Learning (Off-policy TD(0)) to a mobile robot in the Webots 3D physics engine. Our objective is to establish an optimal, mathematically verifiable navigation and obstacle avoidance policy in a 1.2m × 1.2m indoor arena.

2. System Architecture: Webots Controller ↔ Python RL Engine​

The system is decoupled into two clean tiers: the Webots simulation server and the Python RL client.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Webots["Webots 3D Simulator (localhost:5000)"]
        Robot["Supervisor Robot<br>(Ultrasonic Sensor + Wheels)"]
        HeadScan["Head-scan Mechanism<br>(Left/Right 1.1 rad servo)"]
        Server["TCP Socket Server<br>(Line-delimited JSON)"]
        Robot -→ HeadScan -→ Server
    end

    subgraph Python["Python RL Engine (Client)"]
        Env["WebotsEnv (gym-like)<br>reset() / step()"]
        Disc["Discretizer<br>(Continuous → 0~647 Bin)"]
        Agent["QLearningAgent<br>(Q-Table 648x4)"]
        Env -→ Disc -→ Agent
    end

    Server <-→|"request: {type: step, action: 0..3}<br>response: {state: [...], reward, done}"| Env
  • Webots Controller (RL_controller.py): Executes action commands for 480ms (15 simulation ticks × 32ms) and rotates a head-mounted ultrasonic sensor left and right by 1.1 rad ($\approx 63°$) to eliminate blind spots.
  • Socket Protocol: Lightweight line-delimited JSON over TCP localhost:5000:
    • Request: {"type": "step", "action": 0} (0: Forward, 1: Backward, 2: Turn Left, 3: Turn Right)
    • Response: {"state": [0.45, 0.12, 0.35, 0.28, 0.40], "reward": 0.05, "done": false, "info": {...}}

3. Discretizing Continuous Sensors into 648 States​

To apply tabular Q-learning, continuous floats must be mapped into finite discrete states. We selected 5 crucial observation variables based on kinematic relevance:

FeatureBinsThresholdsSemantic Meaning
goal_distance3[0.6m, 1.2m]Near, Mid, Far
goal_heading8[-π, π] (8 sectors, 45° each)Front, Front-Right, Right, Back-Right, Back, Back-Left, Left, Front-Left
front_distance3[0.15m, 0.30m]Danger/Collision, Caution, Safe
left_distance3[0.15m, 0.30m]Danger, Caution, Safe
right_distance3[0.15m, 0.30m]Danger, Caution, Safe

Total State Count: N_states = 3 × 8 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 648

The resulting Q-Table requires only 648 × 4 = 2,592 floating-point entries, allowing sub-millisecond memory updates and zero GPU overhead.

💻 State Discretization Code (discretizer.py)​

import numpy as np

# Dimension boundaries
N_GOAL_D, N_GOAL_H, N_FRONT, N_LEFT, N_RIGHT = 3, 8, 3, 3, 3
N_STATES = N_GOAL_D * N_GOAL_H * N_FRONT * N_LEFT * N_RIGHT  # 648

_HEADING_BINS = np.linspace(-np.pi, np.pi, 9)[1:-1]
_NEAR_BINS    = np.array([0.15, 0.30])
_DIST_BINS    = np.array([0.6, 1.2])

def discretize(state_dict: dict) → int:
    """Maps 5-tuple continuous sensor readings to an integer in [0, 647]."""
    gd = int(np.digitize(state_dict["goal_distance"], _DIST_BINS))
    gh = int(np.digitize(state_dict["goal_heading"], _HEADING_BINS))
    df = int(np.digitize(state_dict["front_distance"], _NEAR_BINS))
    dl = int(np.digitize(state_dict["left_distance"], _NEAR_BINS))
    dr = int(np.digitize(state_dict["right_distance"], _NEAR_BINS))

    # Compute flattened 1D index
    index = ((((gd * N_GOAL_H + gh) * N_FRONT + df) * N_LEFT + dl) * N_RIGHT + dr)
    return int(index)

4. Head-Scan Mechanism & Collision Logic​

A fixed forward-facing sensor leaves lateral blind spots. We implemented an active Head-Scan routine:

  1. Step Execution: Drive motors at 3.0 rad/s for 480ms.
  2. Head Rotation: Sweep head servo +1.1 rad to read left distance, then -1.1 rad for right distance.
  3. Re-center: Return head to 0 rad and refresh front distance.
  4. Terminal Conditions:
    • Goal Reached: Euclidean distance ≤ 0.10m → success (done = True, reward $+1.0$)
    • Collision: Any distance ≤ 0.08m → failure (done = True, reward $-1.0$)

5. What's Next?​

With the simulator environment, TCP socket IPC, and 648-bin state discretization established, our agent is ready for reinforcement learning.

In Episode #2, we will cover the mathematical implementation of Tabular Q-Learning, ε-greedy exploration decay, and reward function tuning!

On top of this, server storage issues forced us to urgently migrate the project's base path from ~/home/ to ~/home/data/temporary/, causing a huge fuss to modify all script paths.

Falling into the Trap of Hardcoding​

After painstakingly running all the evaluation codes, I discovered a horrifying fact.

"Why is MODEL_ALIAS hardcoded to 'Qwen35-9B_a16' in 20_eval_ft_models.ipynb?" "So in the server logs, even for 20_eval_HCX-Text-1p5B_a8.ipynb, MODEL_ALIAS was defined as 'Qwen35-9B_a16'. You're telling me it's normal that the filename and model name are different?"

Yes. While writing the evaluation automation script, I accidentally hardcoded MODEL_ALIAS. The script diligently copied files to test the HCX model, but inside the code, it kept repeatedly loading only the Qwen35-9B_a16 model and doing the same inference over and over!

It was a day that made me realize once again that fine-tuning is not a science, but a battle of meticulousness. I'll have to fix this hardcoded bug and run the inferences again tomorrow.
